stories.title: Garvaghy residents urge PSNI's Boutcher to stop 'hiding'
stories.summary: The Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition is seeking a meeting with PSNI Chief Constable Jon Boutcher as it continues its bid to stop a contentious Orange Order march at Drumcree. Hundreds of people packed into a hall near the Garvaghy Road last night to be told about the outcome of earlier talks held with Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant, however the media were not given access to the meeting. Speaking afterward, association representative Breandán MacCionnaith said he wanted to meet Chief Constable Boutcher, adding he should "stop hiding" and come and meet the people directly affected by the planned parade. He said the vast majority of them did not want the parade to go ahead, and that the Northern Secretary had been left in no doubt about that. Mr Mac Cionnaith had earlier said it was "debateable" if progress had been made in that meeting, adding it was only fair he informed residents of the developments first. "The Secretary of State was left with absolutely no illusions about what the position of this community is," he said.

stories.title: Boiler scrappage scheme among new expanded energy grants
stories.summary: The Government has approved a significant expansion of home energy grants, including a new additional €2,000 payment to encourage households to scrap fossil fuel heating systems and switch to heat pumps or other renewable heating. It has also approved a new €600 grant for domestic battery storage, while some lower-income households will be eligible for grants of up to €9,000 to install solar panels and batteries. The measures are part of a package of enhanced retrofit and renewable energy supports announced by the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment, Darragh O'Brien. Most will begin to open from October, although the new €2,000 boiler scrappage scheme will not come into effect until early next year. However, all eligible homeowners with a heat pump application already in progress will be given the additional boiler scrappage grant of €2,000. The Government says the changes are intended to reduce household and business energy bills, accelerate the move away from imported fossil fuels and make renewable energy technologies available to a wider range of households.

stories.title: Senior Govt figures meet to finalise Budget details
stories.summary: A meeting of Coalition leaders ahead of next week's Budget has concluded at Government Buildings. It is understood a proposal to raise the weekly State pension by €7.50 was still on the table for the party leaders, despite it falling below last year's rise of €10. This was "in order to do more in other areas" one Coalition source stressed, while it is understood there was no discussion tonight of the potential to introduce energy credits. Some Government backbench TDs privately voiced concern today over the increase in the pension not matching last year's figure while also expressing support for some form of targeted one-off payment to help householders with rising energy bills. The leaders also discussed extending the rent-a-room scheme to incentivise people to rent out more than one room. At present, homeowners can let a room tax-free up to €14,000 although this threshold could rise to €20,000.

stories.title: Unemployment rate unchanged at 5% in September - CSO
stories.summary: New figures from the Central Statistics Office show that the unemployment rate was unchanged at 5% in September compared to August. The jobless rate was up from 4.9% in September of last year, the CSO added. Today's figures show that the monthly unemployment rate for men in September stood at 4.9%, up from 4.8% in August but unchanged from the September 2025 revised rate. The monthly jobless rate for women was 5.2%, unchanged from the revised rate in August and up from 4.8% in September 2025. Meanwhile, the youth unemployment rate rose to 12.5% from the revised rate of 12.4% in August. The CSO said the seasonally adjusted number of people who were without a job stood at 149,500 in September, compared with 148,600 in August.

stories.title: Brexit 'did more harm than good' - Burnham
stories.summary: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham faces pressure to commit Labour to rejoining the EU after he promised to look at all options for a closer relationship with the bloc. In his speech to the Labour Party conference today, the Mr Burnham said Brexit had done "more harm than good" and called for Britain to consider its "long-term relationship" with the EU. He announced that he would use the UK-EU summit expected later this year to set out what he believed were the "different options" and attempt to find a political consensus on a way forward. Responding to the prime minister's speech, Labour MP Stella Creasy said "everything must be on the table", including removing the "red lines" set down in the party’s 2024 manifesto that bar rejoining the EU’s single market or the customs union. She said: "Removing the red lines on Europe is the essential first step to restoring this country’s place on the world stage. "We stand with this Prime Minister in making the changes that truly live up to the challenges of 2026, not 2016."

stories.title: Ireland to make Aviva return for Women's 6N clash
stories.summary: The IRFU have confirmed that the Ireland women's side will return to Aviva Stadium in 2027 for their Six Nations clash with England next May. The world champions have never played in Lansdowne Road before, and will enter the clash as the defending Six Nations champions. Ireland played their first standalone women's Six Nations fixture at the venue earlier this year, drawing a crowd of over 30,000 as they defeated Scotland to finish third in the table. Now Scott Bemand's squad will have the chance to do it all again next year, where a bumper crowd will once again be expected. Ireland will open their championship against Scotland at Scottish Gas Murrayfield on Saturday, 10 April (5pm), before returning home to Galway a week later to take on France at Dexcom Stadium on Saturday, 17 April (2.30pm). Bemand's side will then travel to Wales in Round 3 on Saturday, 24 April (12.30pm) before welcoming England, the reigning champions, to Aviva Stadium on Saturday, 8 May (2.45pm).

stories.title: Heimir hits out at 'lies' as squad welcomes Bazunu back
stories.summary: Heimir Hallgrimsson claimed that "a lot of lies" had been written about the situation within the Republic of Ireland camp as he emphasised that the player had welcomed Gavin Bazunu back with open arms in the wake of his decision not to partake in the UEFA Nations League games against Israel. Bazunu was the only absentee for Sunday's 3-0 victory over the Israelis in Debrecen, Hungary. On the eve of the game, the goalkeeper said " it would be wrong to participate in the upcoming fixtures against Israel" and that his decision to sit out the game was a stance "against the atrocities in the region". Reports on Saturday had suggested that the timing of his decision to pull out of the squad had not sat well with some within the Irish camp. Although Bazunu will not play in this Sunday's 'home' game with Israel in Backa Topola, Serbia - a game which Hallgrimsson confirmed will be fulfilled - the Bolton Wanderers player trained with his Ireland team -mates at Aviva Stadium yesterday ahead of Thursday's home fixture against Austria. Speaking in Wednesday's pre-match press conference, Ireland manager Hallgrimsson was keen to laud Bazunu's attitude.

stories.title: Leinster need to bounce back after opening day defeat
stories.summary: It was a disappointing opening weekend of the United Rugby Championship for the Irish provinces. It is the first time in 17 years that all four teams have lost on the opening day of the season. Munster and Connacht were ahead for large periods of their respective games before frustratingly allowing those leads to slip away. Both struggled to hold on in the final quarter, highlighting some of the concerns around quality and squad depth in Irish rugby at present. Ulster, meanwhile, gave Edinburgh too much of a head start before launching their own fightback and coming within a score in a tight finish. The contrast between their start and finish will frustrate head coach Richie Murphy, but the fact that they finished the game playing their best rugby should provide some encouragement ahead of their second-round clash with Glasgow Warriors. Despite losing their opening fixture, Leinster will probably be the happiest of the four provinces after fighting to secure two points away to the Lions. Losing on the opening weekend immediately puts pressure on a team, and it will not get any easier for Leinster when they face the Sharks in the second round. However, there is plenty for Leo Cullen and his coaching staff to be pleased about. They have got the South African trip out of the way early in the season, and in many ways, this could be the perfect time to take an extended squad away for two fixtures.

stories.title: Síomha and the artists saying 'I'm out' to the music industry
stories.summary: Freelance journalist and broadcaster, writing about music and the arts. Putting something you’ve created out into the world inevitably comes with a degree of vulnerability. Anyone who has ever made something and watched it leave their hands will recognise the feeling behind Irish musician Síomha’s latest post on Substack, titled ‘Goodbye social media. Goodbye music industry’. In it, the County Clare native eloquently explained to her fans and readers that she had made a decision to take control over her music and how the industry’s narrow parameters - particularly for independent musicians - had forced her to participate in a game that she was no longer interested in playing. "It’s the whole ecosystem around the music, and the constant feeling that making the work itself is never enough," she wrote. "You have to get people to hear it, get people to talk about it, get people to follow you, get people to come to your shows, and then somehow keep them engaged so you can keep doing it. This whole cycle is hard, even when you have a big team within the machine working it for you. Imagine how hard it is when, as a small independent artist with literally no resources, you are expected to do all that work too?" Síomha, who released her excellent debut album Infinite Space last year, revealed that she had been gradually stepping back from the industry, spending less time on social media and had even removed her music from Spotify last year. She was, she said, tired of her output "being shaped by the algorithm" - although she intends to keep making music on her own terms, which are still being defined. It’s perhaps a gut-churningly difficult decision for some, but a hugely admirable one. Here is a musician who wants to make art for the right reasons; not for fame and fortune, but because it’s a way of expressing herself and channelling her lived experience in the hope that it will resonate with other people. Unfortunately, as Síomha has learned, the industry is not always interested in ‘the right reasons’.

stories.title: Tall Tales & Murder cast on the 'dangerous' new show
stories.summary:
Tall Tales & Murder is a show that defies easy categorisation as it takes us from 8th Century Viking Ireland to modern day Dublin gangland. Donal O'Donoghue talks with three of the show’s starry ensemble cast: Aidan Gillen, Ella Lily Hyland and Aisling O’Sullivan. "I don’t know if I want to do any more acting," says Aidan Gillen, running a hand through his hair. It’s not the first time the actor has voiced such thoughts. And yet the man whose marquee CV includes such seminal TV as Queer as Folk, The Wire, Game of Thrones and Love/Hate, knows only to push the boundaries, and himself. So here comes Tall Tales & Murder’s Grinner McNair, a gangster with a treasure map tattooed onto his chest and a lifetime of badness worn into his face. "He’s an unreliable narrator in a world of unreliable narrators," says Gillen of his role in the near-uncategorisable Stuart Carolan drama. "I’m not sure what genre this is: maybe a screwball comedy thriller is the best description? I get to wear a dress. And I’m asleep a lot in the beginning, but don’t put that as the headline! Haha!"

The Zoom chat begins as a dumb show: Aidan, audio-less, messaging that maybe we should do this semaphore-style, before finally we get vision and sound. Then the actor worries that he has nothing to say, or that, more precisely, he will just end up repeating what he’s said before and maybe we should just wrap this now and rerun those old interviews. And yet despite sometimes stumbling for the right answer or idea, Gillen is compelling company, so aware of the artifice of the set-up but also ready to tear it down. "Long ago I used to write down notes in advance of doing these interviews, so I’d have something to say, but then I thought, 'Why am I doing this because there’s no spontaneity in it?’"

In late 2003, I saw the Dubliner on stage in New York in a production of Harold Pinter’s The Caretaker. Patrick Stewart and Kyle MacLachlan co-starred but it was Gillen that bolted you to your seat with a performance famously described as "dangerous" by the play’s author. That Broadway debut was nominated for a Tony and a Drama Desk award and put Gillen on the map. "Everything I’ve done since The Caretaker in New York came from doing The Caretaker in New York," he says now. "The Wire came directly from that and then Game of Thrones came directly from The Wire and so on. And Mojo in London in 1995 was another fork in the road where I took the right fork. Do you take a fork or take a path or is it a prong?"

The fork – or prong – that brought him to Grinner McNair was shaped by his occasional collaborator Stuart Carolan, creator and writer of Love/Hate, who adapted Tall Tales & Murder from the books of Caimh McDonnell. "What Stuart does really well is push the boundaries to the edge of what is acceptable on primetime TV," says Gillen.

stories.title: Over 100,000 public sector workers begin work-to-rule
stories.summary: More than 100,000 public sector workers in areas such as health, education and local authorities have begun industrial action in the form of a work-to-rule. Nurses, civil servants and special needs assistants are among those taking part in the action over delays in agreeing a new public sector pay deal. The Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation (INMO) said the work-to-rule means that its members in the public health service will perform only duties and responsibilities necessary for safe patient care during their rostered hours. "INMO members will not work any additional unpaid hours," the union said. "They will not attend non-clinical meetings, except where attendance is strictly necessary for direct patient care," the INMO added. The action will also involve Fórsa, the country's largest public sector union, and will see special needs assistants, health workers, civil servants and local authority employees refuse to do additional work outside of their normal duties.

stories.title: Man, woman charged with perjury over McGregor appeal
stories.summary: A man and a woman have been charged with perjury following an investigation by gardaí into evidence filed in Conor McGregor's failed appeal against a civil court jury’s finding that he raped Nikita Hand. Samantha O’Reilly and Steven Cummins were brought before Dublin District Court this morning. They have been charged with giving statements in a judicial proceeding which were false and which they knew to be false. Detective Sergeant Maria Cassells told the court Ms O’Reilly, who is 38, was arrested at the couple’s home in Cherry Orchard Green in Dublin this morning. She has been charged with two counts of giving false statements in January and May last year. Detective Garda Padraic Hanley told the court Mr Cummins, who is 39, was also arrested at home this morning. He has been charged with one count of giving a false statement in January 2025. Judge Michele Finan was told the DPP has directed that they both be tried before a jury in the Circuit Criminal Court.

stories.title: EU ministers to discuss energy-saving measures in Dublin
stories.summary: European energy ministers are to hold talks in Dublin tomorrow as the EU looks to cushion the impact of soaring energy prices ahead of a winter that promises to be difficult for consumers. Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen wrote to the 27 member states ahead of the meeting recommending measures to reduce demand for electricity and gas to help contain prices. "I invite you to consider taking or continuing to take measures that can... reduce gas and electricity demand for as long as necessary," he wrote in the letter, seen by AFP. The informal talks, which will be chaired by Minister for Climate, Energy, and the Environment Darragh O'Brien - under Ireland's Presidency of the EU - are not expected to result in major decisions, but will help coordinate action among the bloc's nations. European gas prices have more than doubled owing to the US-Iran war, just as Europe needs to replenish its reserves with winter beckoning. And Brussels wants to avoid countries rushing to fill up their reserves all together as families prepare to turn on their heaters - at the risk of driving prices up further.

stories.title: Tullow Oil loses $196.5m Ghana tax dispute, shares tank
stories.summary: Tullow Oil lost a $196.5m tax dispute with Ghana today after a tribunal rejected the oil producer's claim that the assessment breached its petroleum agreements, sending its shares plummeting. Shares of the West Africa-focused Tullow were on track to record their worst day since December 2019. They were down 45.1% at 10.7 pence this morning, a reaction Panmure Liberum analyst Ashley Kelty called overdone. "The loss of the tax case is not a huge surprise, but the problem is that until they make some decent progress on paying down debt, I can't see long-term survival really for the company," Kelty said. The tribunal found that Ghana's corporate income tax assessment on insurance proceeds received by Tullow between 2016 and 2019 did not violate the agreements and that penalties equal to 100% of the assessment were not covered by their contractual protections. Tullow said it was disappointed with the ruling and would consider its next steps after further engagement with the Government of Ghana. Ghana's Ministry of Finance said in a statement that it would work closely with Tullow to implement the arbitration award in line with Ghanaian law, while taking into account the need to maintain operations at the Jubilee and TEN oilfields and support the investment needed to sustain production.

stories.summary: US President Donald ⁠Trump has said he has offered Iran nothing to end the war, rejecting media reports that cited US officials saying he was willing to ease sanctions and release frozen funds for "concrete" steps regarding Iran's nuclear programme. "This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING," Mr Trump wrote on Truth Social. Axios and CNN both reported, citing unidentified US officials, that Mr Trump was willing to give Iran sanctions relief and free Iranian funds as part of a final deal on the condition that Iran showed "concrete progress" on the nuclear issue. Mr Trump has cited preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear bomb as a key goal of the war, along with ending its ability to attack its neighbours and creating conditions for Iranians to topple their leadership. Iran does not have nuclear weapons and denies it wants to develop them, but argues it has the right to a domestic nuclear energy capacity. Iranian President Masoud ‌Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show "Face the ⁠Nation", said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear programme and other issues, but would not accept "bullying or coercion".

stories.title: Frying pan to the fire: FAI set for Oireachtas appearance
stories.summary: FAI CEO David Courell and director of football John Martin attended the press conference that day in Hungary alongside Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson as the association tried to explain the turn of events that day and how the last link in the chain - the players - had voted to go ahead with the first of the controversial UEFA Nations League fixtures against Israel. They faced searching enquiries from the Irish press pack about how things had come to a head so dramatically. Meanwhile, highly loaded questions were hurled towards Hallgrimsson from a different contingent of journalists elsewhere on the floor. In another media huddle the same night, Cooke also took a swing at the general media coverage about the Israel fixtures. But the need to answer questions is not at an end for Cooke, Courell and Martin this week. Only the location is changing. Instead of the Nagyerdei Stadion, that trio, along with the FAI board's independent chair Tony Keohane, and directors Aoife Rafferty (People & Culture) and Deirdre Ardagh (Legal & Governance), will be heading to Leinster House on Wednesday afternoon to appear in front of a Joint Oireachtas Committee on Arts, Media, Communications, Culture and Sport. Representatives from Sport Ireland will also attend, while two Department of Culture, Communications and Sport officials Cian Ó Lionáin, the assistant secretary general with responsibility for sport, and Ciarán Shanley, the Principal Officer Sports Policy, are also on the list of attendees.

stories.title: Grugan and Morgan retire from Armagh duty
stories.summary: Armagh All-Ireland winners Rory Grugan and James Morgan have retired from inter-county duty. Grugan was part of Kieran McGeeney's squad that claimed the county's second-ever All-Ireland title against Galway in 2024 while Morgan returned to the squad in 2025. Grugan, a former Orchard County captain, left the final with a serious injury, but Armagh still managed to hold out for a narrow victory. The Ballymacnab man made his debut in 2011 in a Dr McKenna Cup win over Down. Morgan's involvement with the squad has been limited in recent years - although he was in the squad for a 2025 Ulster clash with Antrim - with injuries hampering the latter stages of his career. The Crossmaglen defender came onto the county scene in 2013 and made his name as a tight man-marker.

stories.title: Ward gives surprise call-up to Palace midfielder Hopcroft
stories.summary: Republic of Ireland boss Carla Ward has thrown a curveball ahead of the World Cup play-off semi-final against Kazakhstan by calling up 28-year-old Crystal Palace midfielder Shanade Hopcroft. England-born Hopcroft is eligible to represent the Girls in Green through her grandmother Nora Hopcroft, who hails from Tubbercurry, Co Sligo. The former Chelsea academy player has previously lined out for Birmingham City, London City Lionesses and Colorado Buffaloes. Hopcroft's inclusion appears to have nudged Ruesha Littlejohn out of the squad. Littlejohn has been without a club since last May when her contract at Crystal Palace expired. There is a return for Leicester City defender Heather Payne, back in the fold for the first time since the UEFA Nations League promotion/relegation play-off against Belgium a year ago. Captain Katie McCabe and midfielder Marissa Sheva are both suspended for the first leg, while Denise O'Sullivan will not travel with the squad to Astana due to load management. The Gotham FC player is expected to return for the second leg in Cork.

stories.title: Bleyendaal: 'Business as usual' despite Cullen's swansong
stories.summary: Leinster assistant coach Tyler Bleyendaal insisted it was "business as usual" for the coaching staff despite Leo Cullen's announcement that this campaign would be his final one as head coach after over a decade in the role. The reigning URC champions began their season with a narrow defeat to the Lions in a lively encounter in Johannesburg, their 23-year-old scrum half Fintan Gunne running in three tries in a 27-26 loss. It's been known for some time that it would be Cullen's last campaign after his long reign in the hot-seat, during which he has secured six domestic titles and the Champions Cup in 2018. Asked whether this had changed the dynamic in the coaching set-up, Bleyendaal echoed his head coach in dismissing the idea. "Leo's decision was on his terms. We're all very excited for him, whatever he goes onto," Bleyendaal said. "But otherwise it's business as usual for the whole coaching squad anyway.

stories.title: U2 at 50: The 10 best U2 albums of all time, ranked
stories.summary: Freelance journalist and broadcaster, writing about music and the arts. One of the biggest bands of all time has just celebrated their 50th birthday - and along with it, the news that their first studio album in nine years will be released in November. Ahead of Carnaval de Luz’s release, we’re looking back on U2’s back catalogue and figuring out the albums that deserve a place in the top 10. An often-overlooked gem in the band’s canon, this record saw the Dublin foursome team up with Brian Eno - with whom they had first worked on 1984’s The Unforgettable Fire - for this 1995 side project under the name Passengers. As its title suggests, Original Soundtracks 1 was a collection of songs written for both real and imaginary films, and allowed Bono and co. to experiment with an electronic palette with often surprising and occasionally spectacular results. The album also spawned the unexpected hit Miss Sarajevo featuring Luciano Pavarotti, and a collaboration with Howie B (on Elvis Ate America) which later led to the Scottish trip-hop musician co-producing their next album Pop. Eno took the production reins on this 1984 album, alongside Daniel Lanois - the first of the duo’s spectacularly successful team-ups - but really, this was the sound of a band taking a forthright step into stardom. stories.title: Saint Laurent goes for gold with gilded collection in Paris
stories.summary: Jerry Hall and Rami Malek were among the celebrities watching Saint Laurent go for gold at Paris Fashion Week. They were joined by the likes of Hall's daughter Georgia May Jagger, Zoe Kravitz, Eddie Redmayne and more as Anthony Vaccarello unveiled his spring/summer 2027 collection for the French fashion house. Gold biker jackets, bomber jackets, safari jackets and trench coats alongside metallic pencil skirts and dresses came one after another, as Vaccarello dipped some of Saint Laurent's most recognisable designs in the precious metal. The show took place beneath an enormous chandelier, opposite the glittering Eiffel Tower, on a set inspired by the ballroom of the Hotel InterContinental, where Yves Saint Laurent used to stage his couture shows. The first model appeared almost camouflaged against the opulent surroundings in a liquid-gold utility jacket and matching pencil skirt, with a sheer yellow-gold scarf trailing behind her. Pencil skirts have been a recurring silhouette on the SS 2027 runways, but at Saint Laurent they came with the house's familiar proportions of broad shoulders, a sharply defined waist and a long, lean silhouette.

stories.title: Israel flight diverts to Saudi Arabia after pilots fight
stories.summary: A flydubai plane bound for Tel Aviv was forced to land in Saudi Arabia today after an "incident", the airline said, with Israeli media reporting an altercation between the pilots. Flight FZ 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv "experienced an incident while en route. The aircraft has landed safely in Tabuk Airport (TUU) and all passengers are safe and accounted for," the spokesperson for the low-cost carrier said in a statement. However, the airport said the pilot and co-pilot were hospitalised with injuries. Several Israeli media reported that a fight had broken out between the plane's pilots, reportedly causing a distress signal to be activated. Israel's Kan public broadcaster and Channel 12 reported that the Israeli military had scrambled fighter jets after fears of a possible hijacking - with the hypothesis later dismissed. The office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the premier had held consultations on the matter and was "monitoring developments".

stories.title: New Irish language tool to help non-verbal children
stories.summary: A new language tool that allows non-verbal children to communicate in the Irish language is being made freely available online. The Geabaire app uses the dialects and structures of the Irish language and those behind the technology said it is now a global model for other minority languages. The symbol-to-speech technology was developed after the mother of two autistic children, who are both minimally speaking, approached researchers in Trinity College Dublin to ask them if a speech-generating app could be developed for the Irish language. Julia Cummins, who has since become involved with the project and is doing a PhD on its development, said she had the idea after watching her daughter and son, now aged 14 and 10, using English language versions of the technology. "They were using an app where they could press a symbol, it would represent a word and there would be a speech output, and they were able to combine these words into sentences, so they could get their needs met and express themselves and talk about what they were interested in. "But there was no equivalent of that for the Irish language, and it was impossible to adapt the English language version because the structure of Irish is so different," she said.

stories.summary: Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant has travelled to Belfast amid tense scenes in Drumcree where a planned Orange Orange parade has been met with nationalist protesters. Speaking to reporters in Belfast, Mr Bryant said that "nobody wants to go back 28 years". He also said that everyone needs to "double down on compromise". "I don't think there is a single person involved in politics in Northern Ireland that really wants to go back 28, 30 years and relitigate everything and dismantle the Good Friday Agreement." Maintaining the resilience of the political system in Northern Ireland is of key importance, he said. He said: "I think it's all the more important that we have a Parades Commission that is fully functioning. stories.title: UK economy grew faster than thought in second quarter
stories.summary: Britain's economy grew more quickly than previously thought in the second quarter, consolidating its position as the fastest-growing Group of Seven economy in the first half of 2026 before finance minister John Healey's first budget in October. Economic output expanded by 0.5% in the April-to-June period, the Office for National Statistics said today. The reading was slightly stronger than a preliminary estimate for 0.4% growth in gross domestic product. Economists polled by Reuters had expected the 0.4% rise to be confirmed. Today's data showed that Britain's gross domestic product in the second quarter was 1.4% higher than a year ago - revised up from an initial 1.2% estimate. The figures underlined how Britain's economy has shown surprising resilience in the face of geopolitical upheaval and a global bond market crisis, with consumer confidence data riding high. The data pointed to strength across the economy, with output rising in the manufacturing, construction and dominant services sectors.

stories.title: Anthropic to warn investors of AI's 'risks to humanity'
stories.summary: Anthropic plans to caution potential investors in its IPO that advanced AI could pose "catastrophic or ⁠existential risks to humanity," an extraordinary warning by a company seeking to profit from the same technology. The company's IPO prospectus highlights risks associated with its AI models, which it said could exhibit "self-preserving behaviors," including attempts to "resist shutdown," to "conceal or manipulate information" and behaviour "resembling blackmail." "Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm," Anthropic said in the filing. While public companies routinely outline product risks to investors, few, if any, have issued warnings suggesting their technology could cause potential human extinction. Anthropic emphasized both the transformative potential of AI on par with industrialisation and electricity and the irreversible harm it could cause if mishandled. Anthropic and other AI developers, including OpenAI, have faced scrutiny after incidents where experimental systems defied constraints, including a report of an OpenAI model breaching Australia's health-system database.

stories.title: Ward coy on contract talks as reign enters crucial period
stories.summary: Carla Ward was coy on her long-term Republic of Ireland future yesterday as the Girls in Green's World Cup quest comes to the boil. Ward's contract expires at the end of the qualification campaign. It's hoped that will be after next summer's World Cup in Brazil, but Ireland first have to navigate a play-off semi-final against Kazakhstan and then a final showdown with either Poland or Belgium. Last March, the FAI agreed a contract extension with men's boss Heimir Hallgrimsson before the World Cup play-off against the Czech Republic, which Ireland lost on penalties. Ward has frequently spoken about how much she enjoys the Ireland job but there's been little talk of a fresh deal heading towards a huge autumn and winter period. There's also been turbulence in the build-up to the clash with the Kazakhs. The42.ie reported last night that Brian Sorensen will no longer be coming in as an assistant coach. Villa sacked Natalia Arroyo on Tuesday, with Sorensen - a technical advisor at the club - named interim manager until a permanent successor is found. Extending his commitments to the Girls in Green has, it appears, proven a bridge too far.
